newsitem.title: JAPAN: Briton leads Mazda under public's watchful gaze.
newsitem.headline: Briton leads Mazda under public's watchful gaze.

text.p: For Henry Wallace, president of Mazda Motor Corp since last June, being the first foreigner to run a big Japanese company brings the added pressure of managing under the public spotlight.
"Running a big company is obviously hard enough and running it in a cross-cultural situation adds an increased burden," the 51-year old British national said in an interview on Thursday.
"The public interest adds an extra degree of difficulty. I'd prefer not to have it, but I don't have that choice."
Asked whether he enjoys his current situation, he quickly replied with laugh: "No, I cannot say I do."
Wallace was seconded by Ford Motor Co last June when the U.S. automaker boosted its stake in Mazda to one-third.

His moves have been closely followed by the Japanese public, who are curious whether a foreigner can not only function successfully as the head of a big Japanese company but steer it through the many troubles that confront the automaker.
Mazda is renowned for engineering expertise but has faced a shrinking market share since its strategy of becoming a niche maker of luxury cars and distinctive sports cars fizzled.

Wallace moved aggressively to streamline the company's production operations and product line-up, while introducing several Western approaches to management, including a personnel system focused on merit rather than seniority and recruiting new employees on the Internet.
He said the firm will be in the black in the year ended in March and business will improve in the new fiscal year.
"I think the worst is over, although I think we still have a long way to go as a company before I would be comfortable that we are in good shape," he said.

Wallace said language remains a major obstacle. Although he is taking Japanese language lessons, he needs an interpreter when he attends meetings at the company's headquarters in Hiroshima, where discussions are usually conducted in Japanese.
He also bemoaned the slow pace of change in Japan, where relationships stress the need for harmony.

"I think communication is a problem. Although it is improving, I think it is always going to be to some extent an inhibitor, not in terms of the actual need to translate but the fact that there are differences in cultural language," he said.
